name: Yugoslavism
summary: Yugoslavism holds that the South Slavs, above all Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, are one people by blood, language and interest and should be united politically. It grew out of the Illyrian movement and was pursued in the Corfu pact of 1917, the interwar kingdom and, in a socialist form, Tito's brotherhood and unity. Its strands disagreed mainly over whether the nation should be merged into one centralised nation (integral) or be a federation of historical lands.
scope: Yugoslavism is the idea that the South Slavs (above all Serbs, Croats and Slovenes) form one Yugoslav nation and should be united politically. It runs from the Illyrian movement of the 1830s and Strossmayer's and Rački's cultural Yugoslavism, through the Rijeka Resolution, the 1917 Corfu Declaration and the interwar kingdom, where Lampe and Antić and Dragosavljević distinguish integral Yugoslavism (one nation, Pribićević and ORJUNA) from federalist Yugoslavism, to the socialist 'brotherhood and unity' of Tito's Yugoslavia (Tomasevich, Connor). Excludes Serbian and Croatian nationalism as such, Pan-Slavism, and later Yugo-nostalgia.
